```{r setup}
library(risikoR)
```

This article scripts a whole game: setting up the board, taking a turn by
hand, handing the turn to an AI agent, and reading the map.

## The board

`rk_world()` returns the classic 42-territory board as an `rk_map`.

```{r}
world <- rk_world()
world
world$continent_bonus
rk_neighbors(world, "Brazil")
```

Plotting the map alone shows the adjacency graph coloured by continent. Note
Alaska and Kamchatka: the board wraps around, so the segment between them
crosses the whole picture.

```{r}
rk_plot_map(world)
```

Custom boards are welcome; `rk_map()` validates the graph (it must be
symmetric, and every territory must belong to exactly one continent) and lays
out any board you give it on a circle when you supply no coordinates.

```{r}
mini <- rk_map(
  territories = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  adjacency = list(
    A = c("B", "C"), B = c("A", "D"), C = c("A", "D"), D = c("B", "C")
  ),
  continent = list(North = c("A", "B"), South = c("C", "D")),
  continent_bonus = c(North = 2, South = 3)
)
mini
```

## Dealing a game

```{r}
game <- rk_game(c("Red", "Blue", "Green"), seed = 2024)
game
```

Each player is dealt an equal share of the territories and spreads the
standard number of starting armies (35 for three players) over them.

```{r}
summary(game)
```

## One turn by hand

A turn runs in three phases. Every function returns a **new** game, so you can
keep the old one and compare, replay or branch.

### Reinforce

The allowance is one army per three territories, never fewer than three, plus
the bonus for every continent held outright.

```{r}
rk_reinforcements(game, "Red")
```

Placements are a named vector that must account for every army:

```{r}
front <- rk_legal_attacks(game, "Red")
head(front, 3)

placements <- c(rk_reinforcements(game, "Red"))
names(placements) <- front$from[[1]]
game <- rk_reinforce(game, "Red", placements)
game$phase
```

### Attack

```{r}
set.seed(7)
targets <- rk_legal_attacks(game, "Red")
best <- targets[which.min(targets$def_armies), ]
best

game <- rk_attack(game, best$from, best$to)
game$last_battle
rk_owner(game, best$to)
```

The attack is resolved by `rk_battle()` internally, so the same odds apply as
in the combat engine — and `rk_battle_odds()` will tell you beforehand what
you are getting into:

```{r}
rk_battle_odds(best$att_armies, best$def_armies, method = "exact")
```

### Fortify and hand over

One move along a path of your own territories ends the turn.

```{r}
own <- rk_territories(game, "Red")
from <- own[which.max(rk_armies(game, own))]
reachable <- intersect(rk_neighbors(game, from), own)
if (length(reachable) > 0 && rk_armies(game, from) > 1) {
  game <- rk_fortify(game, from, reachable[[1]], 1)
}
game <- rk_end_turn(game)
game$turn
```

## Letting the agents finish it

`rk_ai()` returns a policy — a function of `(game, player)` that proposes an
action. `rk_step()` applies one action; `rk_play()` runs the whole game.

```{r}
bot <- rk_ai("aggressive")
bot(game, game$turn)$action
```

```{r}
set.seed(11)
result <- rk_play(
  game,
  policies = c(Red = "aggressive", Blue = "cautious", Green = "random"),
  max_rounds = 40
)
result
```

The result carries the standings for every round, which makes the shape of the
game easy to see:

```{r, fig.height = 4}
standings <- result$standings
ggplot2::ggplot(
  standings,
  ggplot2::aes(round, territories, colour = player)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "round", y = "territories held", colour = NULL,
    title = "Who was winning, and when"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
rk_plot_map(result$game)
```

## Writing your own agent

A policy is any function of `(game, player)` that returns an action list, so
a new strategy is a few lines. This one always reinforces its weakest
territory and never attacks:

```{r}
turtle <- function(game, player) {
  if (identical(game$phase, "reinforce")) {
    own <- rk_territories(game, player)
    placements <- rk_reinforcements(game, player)
    names(placements) <- own[which.min(rk_armies(game, own))]
    return(list(action = "reinforce", placements = placements))
  }
  list(action = "end_turn")
}

set.seed(5)
turtle_result <- rk_play(
  rk_game(c("Red", "Blue"), seed = 5),
  policies = list(Red = rk_ai("aggressive"), Blue = turtle),
  max_rounds = 25
)
turtle_result
```

Turtling does not work. Neither does anything else, reliably — which is why
`rk_tournament()` exists.

## The app

`rk_run_app()` opens a four-tab Shiny application: play against the agents on
a clickable map, analyse a single duel, simulate battles against the exact
solution, and run tournaments in the strategy lab.
